voiceover.text: Last time, we saw that a service can be free and still out of reach. But why do some groups need so much more help in the first place? Here's a puzzle. Two babies are born in Australia on the same day, in the same hospital, and both are healthy. On average, one can expect to live around four to five years longer than the other. What would you want to know to predict which one? And how many of those things will either of them ever get to choose?

scenes.title: five groups, from society down to the body

voiceover.text: The things that shape health are called determinants, and the syllabus sorts them into five groups. They act in order, from society down to the body. Broad features of society come first, like culture, education systems, jobs and the media. Then environmental factors, like housing, transport and safe places to walk. Then socioeconomic characteristics, like income, education and occupation. Then health behaviours, like diet, exercise and smoking. And last, biomedical factors, like blood pressure and weight. A clinic treats the bottom of the stack. But the top is what moves a whole population.

These groups don't act one at a time. They interact, in three ways. The first is a chain, where one determinant produces the next. Take a rural community. Specialist services and jobs are concentrated in the cities. That puts care a long way away. Distance makes seeing a specialist cost a day's pay and petrol, so people put it off. And when they finally go, the condition is further along. Every link is ordinary. The chain is what does the damage.

The second way is clustering. Disadvantages tend to arrive together, low income with insecure housing, risky work and poor transport. Because they cluster, their effects compound, so together they do more harm than each would alone. The third way is feedback. Illness makes it harder to work, which cuts income, which worsens the conditions that caused the illness. Put all this together across Australia, and you get the social gradient. Health improves at every step up the income ladder, not just at the bottom. So this isn't only about poverty. It's about how resources are spread across everyone.

Now, the risky behaviours in the middle of the stack. Why do some groups smoke more, or eat worse? The syllabus asks for sociological causes, which means people's situations, not their character. There are five. Norms: where most people around you smoke, smoking takes no decision, and not smoking does. Stress: when money or housing is insecure, short-term relief is worth a lot, and smoking or comfort eating does give relief. Availability and marketing: what's cheap and close is what people eat. Control: prevention is an investment in a future you have to believe in. And belonging: some behaviours are part of fitting in.

That doesn't mean people have no responsibility. People in the same situation do make different choices. The point is that behaviour is patterned. It follows groups, and patterns have causes at the level of the group. So telling people to choose better misses the real constraint, which is often stress, price, environment or belonging, not a lack of knowledge.

So where are the gaps in Australia? Health reports keep pointing to the same groups. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, where the causes are historical and structural, colonisation, dispossession and continuing disadvantage, not cultural. People in rural and remote areas. People with low incomes. People with disability. And some culturally and linguistically diverse communities. Two cautions. These groups overlap, and where they overlap, disadvantage compounds. And no group is all the same. Each gap passes last video's test. It's avoidable, unnecessary and unfair.

Here's the most surprising idea in this topic. Picture a campaign that just gives information: eat more vegetables, walk more. To act on it, people need money, time, transport and security, the very things the determinants spread unevenly. So the better-off group improves faster. The average goes up, so the campaign looks like a success. But the gap gets wider. The fix isn't to drop information. It's to pair it with changes to conditions, like the price and availability of healthy food, safe streets and nearby services, and to target help by need.
Two lines to remember. Upstream shapes health, and downstream is where it gets treated. And a campaign that needs resources to act on helps the people who already have them first.

Two exam questions. First. A national campaign gives every young person a free fitness app with home workout plans. Explain how this campaign could improve the national average, while widening the gap between groups. Pause here to answer.

Using it needs a phone with data, space at home and spare time, and those are spread unevenly by the determinants. So better-off groups take it up more and improve faster. The average rises, but the worse-off group gains less, so the gap widens. The classic mistake is assuming that if the average improved, everyone did.
Second. Explain how determinants of health interact to affect the health of a population group. Pause here to answer.

Stay with one group, like a rural community. Build a chain with a mechanism on each link, from services in the cities, to distance, to cost, to delayed help, to later diagnosis. Then add clustering, because disadvantages arrive together and compound. Add feedback, because illness cuts income. And finish with the social gradient. The classic mistake is five paragraphs, one per determinant, that never interact.

So when a group has worse health, start upstream, follow the chain down, and look for clustering and feedback. And when you judge a campaign, ask who improved, not just whether the average moved. Next, we'll point this same chain at one age group, young people, and ask what's really changed since their parents' generation.
